---
title: "About this site"
---

This site compares two sets of near-real-time quality control flags over the
same ocean profile observations:

- the flags that **came with the input data**, written by whoever produced it, and
- the flags **[`nrtqclib`](https://nrtqclib.readthedocs.io/en/latest/) computed** by
  running the automated Argo/CTD real-time tests (RTQC2 to RTQC14) over the
  same measurements.

Every observation falls into one of four cases, and those four cases are the
colours used throughout:


| Case | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Both flagged | The two sources agree that the observation is bad. |
| Original only | The input data flags it; `nrtqclib` does not. |
| nrtqclib only | `nrtqclib` flags it; the input data does not. |
| Neither flagged | The two sources agree that the observation is good. |

A fifth case, "no input flag", covers observations whose input flag is missing
or unreadable **and** which `nrtqclib` did not flag either: there is nothing to
compare, and they are kept visible rather than folded into "neither flagged".
An observation with no input flag that `nrtqclib` *did* flag counts as "nrtqclib
only", because hiding a computed flag on the grounds that the input said
nothing would defeat the point of the comparison.

## What is published here

**Profiles that neither source flags are not on this site.** A profile is
published only when at least one of its observations, of temperature or
salinity, is flagged by at least one source:

- by the input, with a value the build counts as an anomaly (see
  [Flag values](#flag-values) below), or
- by `nrtqclib`, with any flag above 1 (good).

Everything else is left out: a profile both sources call good throughout,
and also one whose input flags are only values that count as usable or say
nothing (such as 2 probably good, or 9 missing) while `nrtqclib` passes it. Such a profile carries no
disagreement to show, and leaving it out keeps the site small enough to run
in the browser.

The trimming is by profile, not by observation: once a profile qualifies,
all of its observations are published, the good ones too, because a flagged
point is only readable next to the unflagged ones above and below it. That
is why "neither flagged" is still the largest case in the tables.

Every count on the Dashboard, [Regions and products](summary.qmd) and
[Platforms](platforms.qmd) pages therefore describes the published
profiles, not the source dataset. Regions and products shows how much of
each dataset that is, beside the number of profiles that were considered.
The Analyses pages are the exception: they are computed where the data is,
from every profile of the input, and each says which profiles it counts.

## How it runs

Everything is static. The page holds no server-side code: it fetches parquet
files and runs SQL against them in your browser with DuckDB compiled to
WebAssembly. Nothing you click is sent anywhere.

## Flag values

Both flag columns use the IOC/Argo scheme, where 1 means good, 2 probably
good, 3 probably bad and 4 bad; 0 and 9 carry no judgement at all, meaning no
QC was performed and the value is missing. The computed flag always follows
the scheme, and the contingency tables on the dashboard print these words
under the numbers.

Which values of the *input* flag count as an anomaly is a per-variable setting
of the build, listed as `bad_flag_values` in `data/catalog.json`, because
input datasets differ in how they use the upper values. That is what the red
marks in the contingency table, and it is why a number alone cannot say
whether an observation counts as flagged here: the same 6 can be an anomaly
in one product and not in the next.

## The checks `nrtqclib` runs

The computed flag is not one test but twelve. Eleven of them implement the
Argo/CTD real-time tests, and the twelfth is a propagation rule. Each writes
a flag of its own, and `temp_nrt_flag` and `psal_nrt_flag`, the values
compared on this site, are the most severe flag among the checks that apply to
that variable.

| Test | Column | What it looks for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| RTQC2 | `qc_impossible_date` | The profile time is present, later than 1950, and not in the future. |
| RTQC3 | `qc_impossible_location` | Latitude within [-90, 90] and longitude within [-180, 180]. A missing position fails. |
| RTQC4 | `qc_position_on_land` | The position is at sea, read from a sea floor depth column carried by the input. |
| RTQC6 | `{var}_qc_global_range` | The measurement is inside a gross worldwide range: temperature -2.5 to 40 degC, salinity 2 to 41. |
| RTQC7 | `{var}_qc_regional_range` | The same, against the tighter range configured for the region. |
| RTQC8 | `qc_pressure_increasing` | Pressure increases down the profile. Repeated and reversed pressures are flagged. |
| RTQC9 | `{var}_qc_spike` | The value differs sharply from both vertical neighbours, in size and in gradient. |
| RTQC11 | `{var}_qc_gradient` | The step from the vertical neighbours is too steep for the depth. |
| RTQC12 | `{var}_qc_digit_rollover` | A jump from the previous observation big enough to be a sensor wrapping around its range. |
| RTQC13 | `{var}_qc_stuck_value` | Every measurement of the variable in the profile is identical, which is a stuck sensor. |
| RTQC14 | `{var}_qc_density_inversion` | Potential density (sigma-0) falling with depth by more than 0.03 kg/m3. Temperature and salinity are flagged together. |
| (none) | `psal_qc_temp_to_psal` | Not a test: where the final temperature flag is 3 or 4, salinity inherits it at the same severity. |

: {tbl-colwidths="[10,30,60]"}

`{var}` is `temp` or `psal`: a check that reads one variable writes one column
per variable, and one that reads the profile or the pressure writes a single
column shared by both. The gaps in the numbering are real-time tests
`nrtqclib` does not implement.

RTQC2, RTQC3, RTQC4 and RTQC13 judge the profile as a whole, so their flag is
the same on every observation in it. The rest judge one observation at a time,
which is why a spike or a density inversion shows up as a few marked points in
the plots rather than a whole cast.

Which checks ran is a setting of the `nrtqclib` run, not a fixed list, so the
columns present in the data are the checks that were switched on for it: a
check listed above can be missing from a product whose run left it out, and
nothing here will claim otherwise, because the columns are what this site
reads. The **nrtqclib QC checks that flagged** panel on the dashboard names the
ones that fired for the selected profile, in words and by column name, and
links back to this table. Hovering a marker on the plots narrows that to a
single observation: the box names the check or checks that set its computed
flag, and any others that fired below them. Their default thresholds and the
settings that change them are in the [`nrtqclib` NRT QC
guide](https://nrtqclib.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tutorial/running_nrt_qc.html), which is
the source this table summarises.
